section.title: The Angel and the Little Scroll
section.sectionRationale: Between the sixth trumpet and the seventh, John pauses the sequence of judgments for a narrative interlude, just as he did between the sixth and seventh seals. A mighty angel descends with a small open scroll, seven thunders speak and are sealed up, and John is told to eat the scroll and prophesy again. The scene answers Daniel's sealed visions with an unsealed commission, and it prepares the reader for the two witnesses and the seventh trumpet that follow.
section.thesis: Before the last trumpet sounds, heaven interrupts the sequence of judgments to recommission its prophet: some things are sealed and left with God, but the core message, sweet to receive and bitter to carry, must still be preached to the nations.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the mighty angel descending with the little scroll; the seven thunders that speak and are sealed; the angel's oath that the mystery of God will soon be fulfilled without further delay; and John eating the scroll, sweet then bitter, and being sent to prophesy again.

units.label: The mighty angel and the little scroll
units.note: an open scroll, planted on sea and land

verses.text: Then I saw another {{ischyros|mighty}} angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow above his head. His face was like the sun, and his legs were like pillars of fire.
He held in his hand a {{biblaridion|small scroll}}, which lay open. He placed his right foot on the sea and his left foot on the land.

units.label: The seven thunders sealed
units.note: some things are for God alone to know

verses.text: Then he cried out in a loud voice like the roar of a lion. And when he cried out, the seven thunders sounded their voices.
When the seven thunders had spoken, I was about to put it in writing. But I heard a voice from heaven saying, "{{sphragizo|Seal up}} what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down."

units.label: The oath of no more delay
units.note: the mystery of God will be fulfilled

verses.text: Then the angel I had seen standing on the sea and on the land lifted up his right hand to heaven.
And he swore by Him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and everything in it, the earth and everything in it, and the sea and everything in it: "There will be no more delay!
But in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he is about to sound his trumpet, the {{mysterion|mystery}} of God will be fulfilled, just as He proclaimed to His servants the prophets."

units.label: Eating the scroll and the call to prophesy again
units.note: sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach

verses.text: Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, "Go, take the small scroll that lies open in the hand of the angel standing on the sea and on the land."
And I went to the angel and said, "Give me the small scroll." "Take it and eat it," he said. "It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be as sweet as honey."
So I took the small scroll from the angel's hand and ate it; and it was as sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it, my stomach turned bitter.
And they told me, "You must {{propheteuo|prophesy}} again about many peoples and nations and tongues and kings."

ischyros.gloss: Strong, mighty, powerful. It describes this angel's overwhelming, almost theophanic appearance, wrapped in cloud, crowned with a rainbow, face like the sun, legs like pillars of fire. The word signals that this messenger carries the full weight and authority of heaven's presence.

biblaridion.gloss: A little scroll or booklet, the diminutive of biblion. It is deliberately smaller and different from the great sealed scroll of chapter 5 that only the Lamb could open. This little scroll lies already open, ready to be received, eaten, and proclaimed.

sphragizo.gloss: To seal, to close up and mark as secret or reserved. Here it is used negatively, John is told to seal up, that is, to withhold, what the seven thunders said, unlike Daniel, who was told to seal his visions for a future day. Some revelation is given for the church to keep and proclaim; some is entrusted to God alone.

mysterion.gloss: A mystery, a truth once hidden and now to be disclosed at God's appointed time. The mystery of God is not a puzzle to be solved by clever readers but the long-promised plan of redemption and judgment, which will reach its completion when the seventh trumpet sounds, exactly as He announced through His prophets.

propheteuo.gloss: To prophesy, to speak forth God's word as His authorized messenger. John is commissioned to prophesy again, extending his prophetic task beyond his own generation to many peoples, nations, tongues, and kings, a scope that anticipates the whole world hearing this book's message.

basic.context: Right in the middle of the trumpet judgments, John is given a break in the action. A huge angel comes down from heaven holding a small scroll that is already open. He shouts, seven thunders answer, and John is about to write down what they said, but a voice from heaven tells him to seal it up instead. Then the angel swears that there will be no more delay, that when the seventh trumpet sounds, God's whole hidden plan will finally be brought out into the open. John is told to eat the little scroll: it tastes sweet, but it turns his stomach bitter, and then he is sent out again to prophesy to many peoples and nations.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter is honest about the limits of what we can know. Not every mystery in the Bible is meant to be decoded, the seven thunders are sealed precisely so readers will not chase them. What is given, plainly, is a scroll to be eaten and preached. People disagree over how this interlude fits the timeline of Revelation's judgments, whether it points mainly to the fall of Jerusalem, to the whole church age, to a future tribulation, or to a repeating pattern of prophetic suffering, but the plain center holds across all these readings: God's word must be received and proclaimed even when it costs the messenger something.
basic.originalLanguages: The angel is ischyros, mighty, dressed in the very glory of heaven. He holds a biblaridion, a little scroll, smaller and more approachable than the great sealed scroll of chapter 5. John is told to sphragizo, seal up, what the seven thunders said, keeping it from being written. And the angel swears that the mysterion, the mystery, the long-hidden plan of God, will soon be finished, at which point John is sent to propheteuo, prophesy, once more.
basic.typology: The sweet-then-bitter scroll deliberately echoes Ezekiel's call, where the prophet also eats a scroll that tastes like honey before he is sent to a rebellious house. The sealing of hidden words recalls Daniel, who was told to seal up his visions until the time of the end; here, by contrast, the time has drawn so near that sealing is reserved only for the thunders, while the central message must be opened and spoken.
basic.christ: The mighty angel is never called Christ, and Revelation reserves worship for the Lamb alone, yet the scene serves Christ's purposes: it is His mystery, proclaimed to His prophets beforehand, that is here declared ready to be fulfilled. The pattern of a message that is sweet to receive and bitter to bear mirrors the gospel itself, good news of salvation that also means a cross for those who carry it, just as it meant a cross for the One who first bore it.
basic.god: God is sovereign over what is disclosed and what is withheld. He sends His mighty messenger, He silences the thunders, and He swears by His own eternal life that there will be no more delay. He has already told His plan to His servants the prophets, and He will bring it to pass exactly as promised, however sealed or delayed it may feel from where His people stand.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 2 and 3 show a prophet eating a scroll that is sweet in the mouth before a hard commission. Daniel 12 has visions sealed until the time of the end. And Amos 3:7 says the Lord does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets, the same assurance repeated here.
basic.oneStory: All through Scripture God gives His prophets a message that is a joy to receive and a burden to deliver, and He keeps back what is not yet time to know. This scene stands at the center of Revelation as a reminder that the gospel itself works this way: sweet news of a coming King, bitter in what it costs to proclaim Him, until the day when every hidden thing is finally brought into the light.

context.literary:
Revelation 10:1 to 11:13 is an interlude wedged between the sixth and seventh trumpets, and it follows the same pattern as the interlude between the sixth and seventh seals in chapter 7. Both times, just when the reader expects the next blow, the narrator stops and shows what God is doing for His people. The first four trumpets came as a unit, the fifth and sixth were announced as woes, and now the sequence waits. The reader is made to feel the delay, and then the angel's oath in verse 6 declares that the waiting is over.

The scene is built on a chain of echoes. The angel arrives in clothing borrowed from the throne room: a cloud, a rainbow, a face like the sun. His stance, one foot on sea and one on land, claims everything. The seven thunders answer his roar, and the reader is shown that something was said which will not be told. Then the voice turns the narrative from what John hears to what John must do. From verse 8 the angel is almost a prop; the action is John's taking, eating, and being sent.

The chapter closes with a commission that opens the next section, not with a resolution. John must 'prophesy again,' and chapter 11 is that prophecy beginning at once, with measuring, witnesses, and the trumpet itself. Notice also that verse 7 sets a hinge: 'in the days of the voice of the seventh angel' ties this oath to the end of chapter 11, so chapters 10 and 11 read as a single unit around one promise.
context.historical:
John writes from Patmos, an island in the Aegean off the coast of Asia Minor, where he says he is a companion in tribulation, Revelation 1:9. His readers were small, vulnerable churches in cities that prided themselves on loyalty to Rome. To such people a being who plants a foot on sea and land and swears by the Creator is a striking statement of whose world this is. The sea carried Rome's trade and fleets, and the land carried her roads and legions. The angel stands over both, and he takes his oath by God and not by any emperor.

The first hearers also knew the Old Testament pictures behind the scene. Israel had lived through Ezekiel's exile, where a prophet was handed a scroll to eat and sent to a people who would not listen, Ezekiel 2:8 to 3:11. They knew Daniel's vision, in which a man in linen raised both hands to heaven and swore by 'Him who lives forever' about a time, times, and half a time, Daniel 12:7. Sealing a document was an ordinary act in the ancient world, guarding a message until the proper time, and Daniel had been told to shut up and seal his words until the end, Daniel 12:4.

To a congregation that had seen believers imprisoned or killed, a scroll that is sweet to the mouth and bitter in the stomach was no riddle. It described what hearing and speaking God's word would do to them.
context.canonical:
The chapter leans harder on earlier Scripture than almost any other in Revelation. The eating of the scroll comes from Ezekiel 2:8 to 3:3, where the prophet is told to open his mouth, eat what is given, and then speak to Israel. Jeremiah knew the same experience: 'Your words were found, and I ate them. Your words became my joy and my heart's delight,' Jeremiah 15:16, though the same prophet then complains of pain, Jeremiah 15:17 and 20:9. The sweetness of God's words is sung in Psalm 119:103, and John's meal shows that both the sweetness and the sorrow belong to the prophet's calling.

The oath of the angel is modelled on Daniel 12:7, but with a change: in Daniel the end is sealed and far off, while here the angel announces that the delay is over. The mystery that 'He proclaimed to His servants the prophets' answers Amos 3:7. In the New Testament the word mystery is used for a secret now revealed in Christ, as in Romans 16:25 to 26 and Ephesians 3:3 to 6, and Paul links a mystery to the last trumpet in 1 Corinthians 15:51 to 52. The sealing of the thunders finds a parallel in Paul's being caught up to Paradise, where he heard things that man is not permitted to tell, 2 Corinthians 12:4. Deuteronomy 29:29 already taught that secret things belong to the LORD and revealed things to His people.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wanted his readers to be steadied by two promises that seem to pull against each other. The first is that God keeps secrets. Seven thunders spoke, and John, who was ready to write everything, was stopped. A church that feared it must decode every detail of the future was being freed from that burden. Curiosity about what God has not said is not faithfulness, and the passage gently closes that door.

The second promise is that God has already told His people what they need. The angel's oath is not about hidden content but about the pace of the plan: the delay is over, and the plan announced to the prophets is about to be completed. John's readers were weary of waiting, and the message is that the waiting has an end set by the God who made everything.

Then the chapter turns the hearer into a participant. John does not simply watch; he eats and is sent. The first readers were meant to see that taking in God's word and speaking it again go together, and that the cost of speaking it is part of the job, not a sign that something has gone wrong. This was written to prepare them for opposition, not to satisfy curiosity about the timetable.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records one prophet's experience in one vision. It does not command every reader to eat a scroll, to expect bitterness at a set moment, or to treat the silence over the seven thunders as a rule that nobody may ask questions. What it records is a pattern that other prophets lived: Ezekiel and Jeremiah both ate God's words and carried them to hard hearers.

What does carry forward is the shape of faithful speaking. God's word has to be taken in before it is given out, and it is sweet to the one who loves it, yet it may sit heavily when we see what it means for those who refuse it. Believers who preach, teach, or simply speak of Christ to family and friends can expect both. Equally, the sealed thunders model a limit on speculation. Where Scripture is silent, the right response is trust, not the invention of a private timetable. The command to prophesy again is also worth noting: John's bitter stomach does not release him from the task.

debates.question: Why does John seal up the seven thunders instead of writing them down?

views.label: Deliberate divine restraint
views.case: As with Daniel, who was told to seal up his visions until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4, 9), some revelation is simply not given for this age to possess; the sealing teaches humility, reminding readers that Revelation itself does not claim to unveil every last detail of God's plan.

views.label: A literary marker of urgency without a full timetable
views.case: By keeping the thunders unrecorded, John preserves the sense that history's climax remains genuinely open and pressing rather than a fully charted schedule; the reader is kept from treating the book as a decoded calendar and pointed instead toward watchful readiness.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that the sealing is a form of God's kindness, not a withheld threat; readers should resist confident schemes claiming to unlock every hidden thing and instead trust the God who knows what He has not yet disclosed.

debates.question: How does this interlude relate to the timing of the end, and which interpretive approach fits best?

views.label: Preterist
views.case: The announced end of delay and the fulfilling of the mystery of God are tied to the imminent judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, with the trumpet series unfolding within the lifetime of the first readers, vindicating the persecuted church of that generation.

views.label: Historicist
views.case: The interlude marks a pause within a long sequence of trumpet judgments understood to span the whole church age, situating John's recommissioning at a hinge point within an extended historical unfolding of conflict between Christ's kingdom and its opponents.

views.label: Futurist
views.case: The scene anticipates a distinct future tribulation period still to come, in which the mystery of God, His full and final plan for history, reaches its climax at a yet-future seventh trumpet.

views.label: Idealist
views.case: The vision pictures, in a way true for every age rather than tied to one moment, the church's ongoing prophetic vocation: a message sweet in privilege and bitter in cost, given again and again to God's suffering, witnessing people.

debates.bearing: The schools differ on when the mystery of God reaches fulfillment, but they share the same center: God's purposes will not fail or be delayed forever, and His prophets and people must keep speaking His word even when doing so is costly.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the verse 6 oath. The Greek says chronos ouketi estai, which many older versions render 'there should be time no longer.' The word chronos usually means a span or period of time, and in this context it points to delay, as the BSB has it, since the very next verse speaks of what happens 'in the days' of the seventh trumpet. The oath does not abolish time; it ends the period of waiting. Habakkuk 2:3 had promised that the vision 'will surely come and will not delay,' and the angel announces that the long lingering is over.

In verse 7 the verb for what happens to the mystery is etelesthe, from teleo, to bring to an end or complete. It is an aorist, so the angel speaks of the finishing as certain, a thing as good as done. The same chapter then says God 'proclaimed' the mystery to His servants the prophets, and the verb behind it is euangelizo, to announce as good news, the root of 'evangelize' and 'gospel.' The plan that is completed is the good news itself, announced beforehand. The prophets are called His own slaves, douloi, so they belong to Him and carry His word.

The verb for John's bitter stomach is pikrainō, 'to make bitter.' It is the same verb the book used when the star Wormwood made the waters bitter and many died, Revelation 8:11. The prophet's stomach is made bitter by the same word that, in judgment, makes the springs undrinkable. The word for stomach, koilia, is also the word for the inner life in John 7:38, so the bitterness is felt deep inside.

In verse 11 the commission says John must prophesy 'epi' many peoples, nations, tongues, and kings. The preposition epi is flexible. It can mean 'about,' 'over,' or 'to,' and the BSB takes it as 'about.' The list also varies the usual fourfold formula of Revelation, replacing tribes with kings, so that the powerful are included among those who will hear. The verb dei, 'must,' marks it as divine necessity, the same word used for the things that 'must soon take place,' Revelation 1:1. What God's word requires of His servants is as certain as what it announces.

typology.type: Ezekiel eating the scroll, Ezekiel 2:8 to 3:3
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel was told to eat a scroll written on both sides with lament and mourning and woe, and it tasted as sweet as honey. He was then sent to the house of Israel. John repeats the act, but the scope widens: Ezekiel was sent to one people, John to many peoples, nations, tongues, and kings. The pattern is fulfilled in Christ, the Word who 'became flesh,' John 1:14, who took God's word into Himself without remainder and gave it to the world. The type falls short because both prophets were sinners whose bitterness could slide into anger, as Jeremiah's did, while Christ spoke the Father's word without stain.

typology.type: The man in linen who swears by Him who lives forever, Daniel 12:7
typology.fulfillment: Daniel's messenger lifted both hands and swore that all would be completed after a time, times, and half a time. The angel of Revelation 10 lifts his hand and swears by the same eternal God, but says delay is ended. The correspondence shows the sealed vision of Daniel has reached its season. It is fulfilled in Christ, in whom the mystery is made known, Colossians 1:26 to 27. The type falls short because Daniel's words were sealed and stayed so for his lifetime, while the book of Revelation, by contrast, is told not to be sealed, Revelation 22:10.

typology.type: The sealed word that cannot be written, 2 Corinthians 12:4
typology.fulfillment: The seven thunders are sealed, and Paul likewise heard things that man is not permitted to tell. These are not types in the usual sense, but they show a pattern: God sometimes grants a hearing and then withholds the telling. The line that reaches its fullness in Christ is that nothing God wants His people to know is held back. 'I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you,' John 15:15. The limit is real, but it is not a barrier between God and His friends.

study.christ:
This chapter points to Christ by echo, by role, and by contrast. The angel borrows pieces of the glory John saw in chapter 1: a face shining like the sun, Revelation 1:16, and legs like fire, set beside the feet like burnished bronze, Revelation 1:15. The rainbow reminds the reader of the throne, Revelation 4:3. Most readers conclude that the angel is a created messenger dressed in borrowed splendour, not the Lord Himself, since the angel swears by God and is no one's equal. Others hold that this is Christ appearing in angelic form. Either way, the angel's glory is a reflection, and the one he reflects is the Son of Man. The wise move is to let the passage send us back to the Lord who is clearly Lord, not to build a doctrine on a disputed identification.

The little scroll that lies open ties back to chapter 5. There a scroll sealed with seven seals could be opened by none in heaven or on earth until the Lion of Judah, who is the Lamb, took it, Revelation 5:5 to 7. Here the contents of what the Lamb opened lie open in an angel's hand, ready to be eaten by a servant. The open scroll is a sign that the book Christ opened is now to be spoken. Daniel was told to seal his book until the end; the Lamb has broken the seals, and the time of disclosure has begun.

The prophet's bitter stomach points to Christ by pattern. Jesus Himself said that He must suffer many things, Luke 9:22, and that His followers would be hated, John 15:18 to 20. Paul speaks of filling up in his own flesh what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of His body, Colossians 1:24, and the Lord told Ananias that He would show Paul how much he must suffer for His name, Acts 9:15 to 16. Prophetic speech is cruciform. Revelation 19:10 says the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy, which means the one John is told to speak about is Jesus, and the witness John bears carries the cost His Master bore.

Take care not to push the picture. The scroll is not a code for Christ, and the sweetness is not a type of the resurrection. The link rests on the word of God as Christ's word, on the opened scroll of chapter 5, and on the New Testament's plain teaching that those who follow Him share His sufferings.
study.god:
The oath shows a God who is worthy to be sworn by. The angel does not swear by himself or by the heavens alone but by 'Him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and everything in it, the earth and everything in it, and the sea and everything in it.' The threefold listing mirrors Nehemiah 9:6 and Exodus 20:11. The Creator who made all things is also the one who will complete the plan for them, and the oath links the beginning and the end. The God of Genesis 1 is the God who says the delay is over.

He is a God who speaks and also keeps silent, and holds both in His wisdom. He gives the seven thunders a voice and then seals them, so His speech is not obliged to be fully reported. Deuteronomy 29:29 holds the same balance: the secret things belong to the LORD, but the things revealed belong to us. Worship in this chapter includes reverent acceptance of limits. A reader who has to know everything has not yet learned that He is God.

He is faithful to His promises over long stretches. The mystery is 'just as He proclaimed to His servants the prophets.' The word 'just as' says that nothing He announced has been forgotten. Amos 3:7 teaches that He does not act without telling His prophets, and 2 Peter 3:9 explains that what looks like delay is patience. Here, patience and urgency sit together: He waits as long as it serves His mercy, and then He ends the waiting.

He also treats His servants as partners. He does not do all His speaking Himself; He tells John to take, eat, and go. The honey and the bitterness both come from His hand, and neither means He has lost control. For worship the chapter teaches us to take God's word gladly and also to carry the weight of it, trusting that the One who made sea and land and sky has ordered the pace of history and will bring His plan to completion.

crossReferences.note: The model for John's meal. Ezekiel was told to open his mouth, eat the scroll, and fill his stomach with it, and it tasted as sweet as honey. He was then sent to speak God's words to Israel. John's repetition marks him as a prophet in the line of Ezekiel, widened to many nations.

Jeremiah says that God's words were found and he ate them, and they became his joy. In the verses that follow he speaks of loneliness and pain. The same prophet knew sweetness and bitterness together, which is exactly the double experience John is given.

Daniel was told to shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end. John is the other side of that command: he is told to seal one message, the thunders, but to take and speak another, which signals that Daniel's end-time has come near.

The messenger above the river raised both hands and swore by Him who lives forever about a time, times, and half a time. The angel in Revelation 10 copies the gesture and the oath, but his message is that the long delay is now over and the plan is about to be finished.

The psalmist says God's words are sweeter than honey to his mouth. This is the first half of John's experience, and it shows that the honey is no strange image: Israel's worshippers had long said that to taste God's word is to delight in it.

The voice of the LORD is heard seven times in this psalm, thundering over the waters and shaking the wilderness. The seven thunders recall this picture of God's voice in creation and judgment, and they show that God's speech carries power even where its words are withheld.

The vision awaits an appointed time, and though it lingers it will surely come and will not delay. The angel's oath answers this long-waiting promise, announcing that the appointed time has arrived and the lingering is over.

Paul was caught up to Paradise and heard things too sacred for words, things that man is not permitted to tell. It is the clearest New Testament parallel to the sealed thunders: a real revelation that God chose to keep from the written record.

Paul describes the mystery kept secret for long ages and now disclosed through the prophetic writings by the command of the eternal God. This is what Revelation 10:7 means by the mystery proclaimed to the prophets: God's plan in Christ, long announced and now being brought to completion.

The seventh trumpet that the angel promised sounds in the next chapter, and the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of the Lord and His Christ. The oath of chapter 10 and the announcement of chapter 11 belong together, as promise and arrival.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a God who speaks and a creation that obeys. Genesis 1 is a sequence of commands, and Psalm 29 hears the same voice in the thunder. When the human race fell, the word of God did not stop. It was entrusted to prophets, and one of the great questions running through the Old Testament is how long. How long until the exile ends, how long until the promised king, how long until the nations see? Habakkuk was told to wait, and Daniel was told to seal his book until the time of the end.

Revelation 10 stands at the point where the answer begins to arrive. The scroll that was sealed in Daniel and in Revelation 5 is now open and in the hand of a messenger who plants himself on sea and land, claiming the whole created order for its Maker. The oath of the angel is the story's long delay being cut short.

The chapter also shows the cost of being a part of this story. The same word that is honey in the mouth is bitter in the stomach, because the plan of God does not run through comfortable places. The church is sent to many peoples, and the gospel that gathers a great multitude, Revelation 7:9, also meets rulers who will not hear. John is sent again to those kings, and the bitterness belongs to that sending.

The story ends where the angel promised, at the seventh trumpet and the reign of Christ, and beyond that, in the new creation. In Revelation 22:10 John is told not to seal the words of this prophecy, because the time is near, which reverses Daniel's sealed book. At the end there will be no more mystery withheld and no more bitterness, and God's servants will see His face, Revelation 22:3 to 4.

sermon.title: The Little Scroll
sermon.why: Ferguson preaches directly on Revelation 10:1-11:11, treating the mighty angel, the little scroll, and John's sweet-then-bitter commissioning as the hinge into the two witnesses, matching this study's passage and its themes of prophetic recommissioning.

quiz.q: What does John do with the words of the seven thunders?

options.text: He is told to seal them up and not write them down, leaving them undisclosed.
options.note: Revelation 10:4 records the voice from heaven commanding John to seal up what the thunders said.

options.text: He immediately writes them down and includes them in his book.
options.note: The opposite happens; he is stopped from writing them and told to seal them instead.

options.text: He shouts them back to the angel.
options.note: He is commanded to keep silent about them, not to repeat them aloud.

options.text: He forgets them completely before he can act.
options.note: He remembers them well enough to almost write them down; he is deliberately told to withhold them, not left forgetting by accident.

quiz.q: What does the mighty angel swear concerning the mystery of God?

options.text: That there will be no more delay, and the mystery of God will be fulfilled when the seventh trumpet sounds.
options.note: Revelation 10:6-7 records this exact oath.

options.text: That the mystery of God will never be revealed.
options.note: The opposite is promised; it will be fulfilled, not permanently hidden.

options.text: That the seventh trumpet has been indefinitely postponed.
options.note: He swears the very opposite, that there will be no more delay.

options.text: That only angels, not prophets, will ever understand the mystery.
options.note: The mystery was already proclaimed to His servants the prophets, and John is sent to prophesy it further.

quiz.q: What happens when John eats the small scroll?

options.text: It is sweet as honey in his mouth but turns his stomach bitter.
options.note: Revelation 10:9-10 describes exactly this sequence.

options.text: It is bitter in his mouth but becomes sweet once swallowed.
options.note: The order is reversed from what the text actually says.

options.text: It has no taste or effect at all.
options.note: The text is specific about both a sweet taste and a bitter aftereffect.

options.text: It makes him unable to speak.
options.note: Far from silencing him, eating the scroll leads directly to his commission to prophesy again.

quiz.q: What is John commanded to do after eating the scroll?

options.text: Prophesy again about many peoples, nations, tongues, and kings.
options.note: Revelation 10:11 gives this exact commission.

options.text: Remain silent for the rest of his life.
options.note: The opposite command is given, to prophesy again, not to fall silent.

options.text: Return the scroll unopened to the angel.
options.note: He has already eaten it; he is sent out to speak, not to give it back.

options.text: Seal up everything he has seen so far.
options.note: Only the seven thunders are sealed; the scroll's message must be proclaimed, not hidden.

quiz.q: How does this scene echo the Old Testament prophets?

options.text: It parallels Ezekiel eating a scroll sweet as honey before a hard prophetic task, and Daniel's visions being sealed for a future time.
options.note: Both Ezekiel 2-3 and Daniel 12 stand directly behind this scene.

options.text: It has no connection to any earlier prophet.
options.note: The imagery is drawn directly from Ezekiel and Daniel.

options.text: It rewrites Isaiah's call vision from the temple.
options.note: Isaiah's call involves a burning coal, not an eaten scroll; the closer parallels are Ezekiel and Daniel.

options.text: It borrows only from pagan prophetic rituals.
options.note: The imagery is thoroughly biblical, rooted in Israel's own prophetic tradition.

questions: John was told to seal up the seven thunders rather than write them down. What helps you trust God with what He has not yet explained to you?
The scroll was sweet in John's mouth but bitter in his stomach. Where have you found God's word to be a joy to receive but costly to live out or share?
The angel declared there would be no more delay. How does that promise shape the way you wait through seasons that feel long or unresolved?
John was recommissioned to prophesy again after his hard experience with the scroll. What would it look like for you to keep speaking God's truth even when it has cost you something?
This scene draws on Ezekiel and Daniel to show John standing in a long prophetic line. How does knowing your own calling is part of that same larger story encourage you today?

translationNotes.note: Small scroll (biblaridion) is a diminutive form, deliberately distinguishing this scroll from the great sealed scroll of chapter 5; some translations render it 'little scroll' or 'little book' to preserve the contrast.
Seal up what the seven thunders have said is a direct instruction to withhold, not merely to keep private; the thunders' content is never disclosed anywhere in the book.

There will be no more delay can also be rendered 'time will be no more' in older translations, but the sense in context is the ending of a period of waiting before the mystery of God is fulfilled, not the cessation of time itself.

Sweet as honey, then bitter in the stomach closely mirrors Ezekiel 3:3, and the sequence of taste followed by digestion pictures the difference between receiving God's word gladly and then living out its costly implications.
